title: Black-Eyed Pea Salad
author: Amy Scattergood (adapted from Pierre Thiam)
desc: Black-eyed peas boiled until tender, folded into a bowl of tomato, cucumber, pepper, parsley, lime and habanero with two-thirds cup of olive oil, and rested an hour.
longDesc: Half a pound of black-eyed peas, soaked an hour, boil about 30 minutes in a quart of water until tender, with half a teaspoon of salt near the end. A large bowl holds the diced tomato, cucumber and red bell pepper, chopped green onions and parsley, lime juice, a seeded habanero, the other half teaspoon of salt and black pepper; olive oil is whisked in and the peas folded through. The salad rests an hour ‘so the flavors blend’ and is served in lettuce leaves.
ingredients: 1/2 pound black-eyed peas, soaked in water for 1 hour
1 tsp salt, divided in two parts
1 red bell pepper, seeded and diced
1 habanero pepper, seeded and finely chopped
steps: Boil the soaked peas in the quart of water about 30 minutes, until tender. Add half a teaspoon of the salt near the end of the cooking time.
In a large bowl combine the tomato, cucumber, bell pepper, green onions, parsley, lime juice, habanero, the remaining half teaspoon of salt and the black pepper.
Whisk in the olive oil, then gently fold in the black-eyed peas. Cover and rest for an hour so the flavours blend. Serve in lettuce leaves.
chefTips: ‘Until tender’ is the cue for the peas; salt goes in near the end of cooking.
The hour’s rest is a printed instruction, not an option.
Fold, don’t stir, so the peas hold their shape.
Canned peas are used in the Yolélé derivative with a 10-minute rest; this version uses dried peas.
commonMistakes: Salting the peas at the start of boiling.
reheating: Serve cold or at room temperature.
healthBenefits: Black-eyed peas supply fibre and folate.
culturalNote: The page prints the Wolof-looking name ‘salatu niebe’ but does not identify the language. The Saveur May 2012 feature prints a related ‘Saladu Ñebbe’ at 5 cups of cooked peas, a cup each of canola oil and parsley, and a misprinted ‘1o’ scallions.
sources: Title as printed: ‘Recipe: Black-eyed pea salad’. Local name in the description and body: ‘salatu niebe’ (the language is not identified). PAGE BYLINE: ‘By Amy Scattergood, Los Angeles Times-Washington Post’. CREDITED RECIPE AUTHOR (differs from the byline): ‘Adapted from Yolele! Recipes From the Heart of Senegal by Pierre Thiam’. Publication: gulfnews.com, last updated 15 January 2021. Yield: ‘Servings: 8’. TWO-PASS on every quantity.
Cues in short fragments: ‘until tender’; salt ‘near the end of the cooking time’; ‘so the flavors blend’. No temperatures.

DISAGREEMENTS with the Yolélé derivative ‘Salatu Niebe Salsa’ (yolele.com, 16 July 2024, byline ‘Yolele’, SINGLE-PASS): canned peas rather than 1/2 lb dried soaked and boiled; 1/4 cup olive oil against 2/3 cup; a 10-minute rest against an hour; no black pepper; no lettuce. Not entered separately.
Compare Saveur’s ‘Saladu Ñebbe’ (SINGLE-PASS, May 2012 issue): 5 cups cooked peas, 1 cup canola oil, 1 cup parsley, and ‘1o’ scallions — a suspected misprint kept as printed.
